criteria.remark: Two images, one on each of two pages, carry no text alternative: the hero graphic on the home page and the avatar on the account page. Neither has an alt attribute nor any other text an assistive technology can announce, so a screen reader user receives nothing in place of the picture. Both are confirmed defects on the pages tested; this evidence speaks only to the images encountered there.

Sixteen in-page links across five pages were flagged for a person to judge rather than recorded as failures. What was measured is that activating each one moves nothing: the header link points at "#main-content" and several in-content links point at "#news", and on those pages no element carries the id or name being targeted. What a person has to decide is whether another mechanism bypasses the same blocks — a heading, a landmark or a collapsible block. Several of the sixteen read as ordinary in-content links rather than skip mechanisms. skip-link-works could not look on 1 of 35 scans (the path is replayed once for each rule, and this rule needed its end loaded again); what it would have found is not shown.

This case-id link is what produced the ?upload=BP-2026-10882 state, so it acts as a record control in a td of table.cases rather than a mechanism to bypass repeated blocks.
A case reference in a table row cell of table.cases, the same pattern as the row link that opened the upload view. Not a bypass mechanism for repeated blocks.
Per-row case-id anchor inside tbody of table.cases; it sits within the content and offers no skip over blocks, so the rule's concern does not apply to it.

Eighteen links across six pages have no text a screen reader can announce. Each is an icon-only link whose sole content is a small inline graphic marked as hidden from assistive technology, so the link is reachable by keyboard yet reaches the user unnamed; a repeated set of social-media icon links accounts for the examples on each page tested. For anyone who cannot see the icon, the destination of these links is not available in any form.

Twenty-two elements across six pages expose no name that assistive technology can read. They include icon-only links whose single graphic is hidden from assistive technology, leaving the control nameless in the keyboard tab order, and an entry field for a Social Security number on the application form with no label, title or other text attached to it. Screen reader and voice-control users cannot tell what these controls are or address them by name.

Nine pieces of text across six pages are too faint against their background. The "Last updated" line that recurs from page to page is mid-grey on white at 2.81 to 1, and a "Pending" status badge on the status page is amber on white at 2.27 to 1, against a 4.5 to 1 threshold for text of that size. Readers with low vision, or anyone viewing in bright light, may be unable to make this text out, including the badge, which carries status meaning.

Eight form controls across two pages were flagged for a person to judge. What was measured is the focus outline drawn around each: a pale amber on a white surface at 1.66 to 1, below the 3 to 1 threshold for a visual boundary of this kind. The controls are the first name, last name, date of birth and Social Security number fields and the household size menu on the application form. What a person has to decide is whether another visual cue identifies the focus.
